extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and general readers interested in film publicity, advertising, and media history
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of the history, tactics, and norms of film publicity and advertising from the silent era through the Internet era, describing practices studios, publicists, and exhibitors have used to promote films and stars. Useful for understanding what constitutes a complete promotional campaign and the ethical/regulatory constraints that have shaped it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core components of a film publicity campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: Most important promotional tactics—trailers, print advertisements, press books, posters, promotional tie-ins, star premieres, stunts and gimmicks—constitute a film's publicity and advertising campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comprehensive campaign typically combines multiple elements (trailers, print ads, posters, pressbooks, tie-ins, premieres, stunts). These were in place by 1915 though their forms evolved; modern campaigns continue to use these components adapted to new media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressbook content and function
rubrics_metrics.description: The ad campaign for each film was distilled into a pressbook sent to exhibitors; pressbooks historically contained fake newspaper stories, photos, fashion displays, ideas for stunts, and free posters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pressbooks provide 'everything an exhibitor needed to advertise the film' and list available tie-ins; contemporary pressbooks are simpler (folders with promotional images, cast photos, and a few press releases). Historically they coordinated local stunts and exhibitor materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and conformity to moral/advertising codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Advertising Code, advertisements could not be misleading, false, or quote dialogue out of context and had to conform to the Production Code—nudity, salacious poses, violence, and profanity were banned; publicity could not capitalize on censorship or litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-1930 rules required submission to the MPAA and respect for religion, patriotism, other nations, the law, and the police; fines were imposed for violations. Although no Advertising Code exists today, trailers are industry-regulated and the MPAA recommends avoiding excessive sex, violence, and drug use in trailers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trailers strategy and evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Trailers are used to create anticipation and stimulate advance ticket sales; their form evolved from voice-over heavy to footage-focused, and later to mood/emphasis on unique qualities or stars and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trailers should be tailored to film length, budget, and marketing goals: classical-era trailers emphasized voice-over and superlatives; post-classical trailers often focus on unique qualities or mood; experimentation can pay off (e.g., Rosemary's Baby), but revealing plot twists can be risky and is sometimes justified as a unique selling point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stunts and gimmicks
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotional stunts and gimmicks (contests, giveaways, public reenactments, in-theater gimmicks) are a long-standing tactic to attract attention and create event-like experiences around a film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stunts should align with the film's audience and positioning: examples include Barnumesque theater stunts, William Castle's seat-wiring Percepto, Marilyn Monroe skirt reenactments, insured 'Fright Insurance'—effective for low-budget or youth-targeted releases but may overshadow the film if misused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie-ins and merchandising strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tie-ins are merchandise related to the film (branded goods, toys, clothes, sheet music, soundtrack recordings) designed to bring consumers closer to the movie experience and capitalize on stars and screen imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful tie-ins require alignment with target demographics (historically women and children; some aimed at men), advance coordination with manufacturers (studios submitted sketches up to a year ahead), and brand coherence; long-lived tie-ins (e.g., Shirley Temple dolls, Max Factor cosmetics) demonstrate enduring payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Star image creation and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Studios and publicity departments manufacture and protect star personae via biographies, photo sessions, controlled press, morality clauses in contracts, fan clubs, glamour shots, and by covering up scandals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Star publicity often predates specific films and requires ongoing image testing, press management, rumor control, and strategic off-screen appearances; after the studio era, talent agents and independent publicists assumed many of these functions (often for ~10% of salary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Press relations and supply of promotional materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Studios provided newspapers with press releases and promotional copy, and worked with press syndicates; publicists supplied copy and photos and cultivated cordial relationships with the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining good press relations is essential—studios might pull advertising from hostile papers; providing ready-to-run materials (press releases, photos, feature copy) encourages positive coverage and reuse in fan magazines and local papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized campaign coordination with exhibitors
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically studios consolidated control over advertising so exhibitors used studio-approved materials; poster departments and exploitation departments supplied theaters with posters, tie-ins, and stunt ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinated distribution of promotional materials (posters, lobby cards, pressbooks) ensures consistent messaging; while exhibitors once had latitude, studio-provided campaigns were often mandatory under the Advertising Code era and encouraged uniformity across markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to new media and demographic shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotional strategies shifted in response to new media (radio, television, video, DVD, digital downloads, Internet) and to changing audience demographics (e.g., targeting young adults with pop soundtracks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective campaigns leverage appropriate platforms for the target audience (radio tie-ins in the 1930s–40s, TV spots and televised excerpts mid-century, Internet sites and viral tactics since the 1990s); media choice should reflect where the audience consumes content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet and viral/tease-site tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Web-based campaigns (tease sites, 'authenticity' claims, fake sites, interactive games) serve as anchors for trailers, press info, and audience engagement; the Blair Witch Project exemplified an Internet-era campaign built on claimed authenticity and transmedia elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internet strategies can create pre-release buzz and cross-media synergy (e.g., Sci-Fi Channel specials, fake evidence, missing-person listings). However, novelty and timing often determine success; many elaborate web campaigns function mainly as distribution points for trailers and cast/crew info.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budgeting and scale of promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotional budgets can rival or exceed production costs and historically have been a crucial allocation for studios trying to recapture audiences amid competition from other media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocation decisions should consider cross-media buys, stunts, star appearances, tie-ins, and timing; higher budgets enable broader campaigns (TV spots, national print, large premieres), but strategic low-budget gimmicks can also generate outsized attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eventization and timing (premieres, star appearances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a film a singular event—through star-studded premieres, reenactments, or timing of promotional appearances—boosts visibility and can affect reception and viewing behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premieres and high-profile appearances should be timed to maximize media coverage and tie into other campaign elements; targeted stunts (e.g., blocking admittance after ten minutes for Psycho) can shape audience behavior and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation and content-sensitivity for trailers and ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Trailers and ads are industry-regulated: ratings context matters (a trailer's content should consider the film's rating and what precedes it) and MPAA recommends avoiding excessive depictions of sex, violence, and drugs in trailers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers must tailor trailer/ad content to exhibition contexts and rating constraints; explicit content may be curtailed or edited to meet exhibitor and industry expectations and to avoid alienating audiences or violating guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative press-advertising practices with media partners
rubrics_metrics.description: Studios historically collaborated with major press syndicates and radio networks to promote films (e.g., serial collaborations, radio broadcasts of film excerpts), integrating advertising with editorial and programmatic outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic partnerships with media outlets can amplify reach (serials in newspapers, radio programs featuring film scenes, syndicated stories); studios sometimes provided material that press outlets repurposed as features, increasing public familiarity and cultural standing.
